headline: Number of Young Brits Not in Work or Education Falls to 959,000
author: Irina Anghel

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 26, 2026 at 4:53 AM EST 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- The number of young Britons shut out of work of education declined in the third quarter, offering some relief to Prime Minister Andy Burnham in his mission to fix the UK's youth jobs crisis.

Some 959,000 16-24 year-olds were not in employment, education or training (NEET), down 22,000 from the previous quarter, the Office for National Statistics said Thursday in a report. While that's down from the start of the year when it topped one million, it's still higher than a year ago and close to levels seen in 2013 in the aftermath of the global financial crisis.

Getting young people into work is a key political and fiscal challenge for Burnham. Alan Milburn's landmark 267-page report last week gave the government a roadmap for tackling the issue, setting out measures to cut the NEET rate to 5% over the next decade. The crisis is already costing Britain £125 billion ($164 billion) a year due to lost output, benefit and healthcare costs, foregone tax and long-term scarring, it found.

Milburn urged the government to cut job taxes for under-25s, subsidize firms taking on unemployed young people and avoid more steep rises to the youth national minimum wage. The report also warned that Labour's tougher employment laws are making firms less likely to create entry-level roles.

Underlying Milburn's review is an ambition to shift public spending away from benefits to employment support. He highlighted that the state currently spends £25 on benefits for young people for every pound to help them into education and employment, a ratio he said should be changed to 2:1 over the next decade.

Competition for first-jobs is at its most brutal since the economy was under lockdown during the pandemic. Payroll tax hikes, large increases in the minium wage, elevated interest rates and, more recently, AI advances have created what the Bank of England calls a "low fire, low hire" labor market that's particularly taxing for young people.

"I suspect I'm not the only person whose first job was in a shop," BOE Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli told lawmakers on Wednesday. She said key employers of young people in sectors such as retail and hospitality have scaled back hiring dramatically and warned that a difficult start can hold back workers throughout their careers.
